source.title: Pruning's Effect on Generalization Through the Lens of Training and Regularization
source.authors: Tian Jin; Michael Carbin; Daniel M. Roy; Jonathan Frankle; G. Dziugaite

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no truncation apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests pruning and model-size reduction as influences on generalization, in settings beyond the listed versions’ specified experiments. It does not test the listed versions’ particular claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports pruning, extended dense training, and width down-scaling results on test error and training loss. It does not test random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples as defined in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study tests explanations of pruning’s generalization benefits, not V1–V8. Its width comparisons do not establish behavior beyond the width needed for zero training error; partially corrupted labels do not test the full random-label comparison in V1; and example removal uses pruning-induced loss changes rather than V8’s memorization measure. The record’s T3 classification is therefore incorrect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record’s paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that size reduction alone cannot explain pruning’s generalization benefits: extended training can improve fitting, while size reduction can add regularization against noisy examples. Both effects are needed across the tested settings.
record.recipe_differences: Studies iterative magnitude pruning with learning-rate rewinding, extended dense training, and width down-scaling rather than the claim versions’ specified interventions and setups.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pruning effects vary with sparsity, dataset noise level, architecture-dataset benchmark, pruning algorithm, and whether training time is extended or model width is reduced.

fits_no_version.finding: Extended dense training can reproduce pruning’s generalization benefits on clean benchmarks; noisy-label settings often require additional regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning’s generalization benefits depend jointly on training duration and schedule, sparsity, and label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Width reduction and pruning can mitigate label noise, although their optimal test errors differ by benchmark and noise level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing model size can improve generalization with corrupted labels without fully reproducing iterative pruning’s benefits.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning affects training examples nonuniformly, improving their fit at some sparsities and preferentially worsening noisy-example fit at others.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning’s generalization effects accompany heterogeneous changes in per-example training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix D finds that removing the 20% most improved examples hurts test accuracy more than random removal on four of five benchmarks; the CIFAR-100 difference emerges with a wider ResNet32. Selection uses pruning-induced loss improvement, not memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Examples whose loss improves most during pruning can contribute disproportionately to test accuracy.

record.problems: The study is empirical and the authors caution that findings may not generalize beyond the tested benchmarks. Some comparisons are described as aggregate outcomes or shown in figures; numerical standard deviations are reported in tables, but many prose comparisons do not give uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were extracted from figures that show full sparsity curves without accompanying textual numerical descriptions; figure-only values were not estimated. Appendix D, E, I, J, K, and L contain further experiments on example subsets, algorithm variants, and subgroup losses; these were omitted where they repeat the extracted findings or do not add a distinct directly relevant outcome within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Almost-perfect fitting of fixed fully random labels, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance held-out accuracy under random labels using the same architectures and recipes.
Test-error behavior when widening beyond an established zero-training-error threshold. Width reduction under fixed training schedules does not establish this condition.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Within-benchmark adaptive-versus-SGD comparisons and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, underfitting, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removal of examples selected by inclusion-based memorization scores versus equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures do not identify a listed effect; this does not dispute the pruning findings themselves. Appendix D’s removal experiment is a particularly close but distinct construct from V8. No verdict labels or missing version-bearing results are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same architectures and recipes.
Widening one-hidden-layer ReLU networks beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the specified local-connectivity comparisons.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons and tuning conditions.
Large- versus small-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and the interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to train-test generalization gaps.
Removing examples selected by how strongly their memorization affects their own-label prediction.

rows.subject: LeNet

rows.value: Extended dense training is worse by 0 (matching) to 2.6%.
rows.note: The range is reported over the tested noise levels.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error of width-down-scaled dense models with optimally sparse models.
rows.value: Width down-scaling under-performs pruning on the benchmark; with random label noise, width down-scaling has notable regularization effects and significantly improves generalization.
rows.note: The paper reports a benchmark-level comparison, not individual numerical outcomes here.
rows.check: Split clean and noisy conditions. Table 7 gives WD/LR errors of 1.90/1.82%, 5.63/5.21%, 5.45/7.57%, and 6.08/9.96% at 0/5/10/15% noise: width reduction outperforms pruning at the two highest noise levels. This does not establish V2’s interpolation condition.

rows.subject: ResNet20
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error of width-down-scaled dense models with optimally sparse models.
rows.value: Pruning does better by 0% (matching) on the benchmark at optimal test error; width down-scaling has notable regularization effects with random label noise.
rows.note: The reported difference range for ResNet20 is 0% (matching).
rows.check: The matching statement applies to noisy conditions, not the entire row. At 0% noise Table 7 gives WD 8.42±0.11% versus LR 7.71±0.09%. No zero-training-error threshold is established.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error of width-down-scaled dense models with optimally sparse models.
rows.value: Pruning does better by 1.5 to 1.8% without random label noise; width down-scaling has notable regularization effects with random label noise.
rows.note: The paper reports a range for the pruning advantage.
rows.check: The 1.5–1.8-point prose range concerns noisy conditions, not clean data. Table 7 gives a clean-data difference of 0.81 points and noisy differences of 1.85, 1.96, and 1.47 points; retain the prose/table discrepancy.

rows.subject: ResNet32
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error of width-down-scaled dense models with optimally sparse models.
rows.value: Pruning does better by 0 (matching) to 2.1%; width down-scaling has notable regularization effects with random label noise.
rows.note: The paper reports a range for the pruning advantage.
rows.check: Separate clean and noisy conditions. The prose’s matching-to-2.1-point range describes noisy comparisons; Table 7 gives a clean-data difference of 0.50 points. Neither comparison establishes V2’s interpolation condition.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error of width-down-scaled dense models with optimally sparse models.
rows.value: Pruning does better by 0.36%; width down-scaling has notable regularization effects with random label noise.
rows.note: The reported difference is at optimal test error.
rows.check: The prose’s 0.36-point advantage conflicts with Table 7: WD/LR are 23.89/23.42% without noise and 24.75/26.15% with 15% noise. Width reduction is better by 1.40 points in the noisy condition. Split conditions and flag the discrepancy.

rows.operation_detail: Compared subgroup training loss on original and random-label examples as sparsity increased.

conditions.value: MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet with injected random label noise

rows.baseline: Dense model trained with standard training
rows.value: At ranges of sparsity where generalization improves, sparse models fit original examples significantly better than randomized-label examples; the paper reports the loss gap widening from 0.03–0.13 to 1.38–2.97 for dense versus optimally sparse VGG-16 on CIFAR-10 with 15%–60% noise.
rows.note: The stated loss-gap ranges are across the reported noise levels.
rows.check: The loss-gap ranges reproduce Section 4, but do not test almost-perfect fitting of fully randomized labels alongside natural-label held-out accuracy. The aggregate also conceals exceptions: Table 11 shows noisy-example loss decreasing for LeNet at 5% noise and ResNet50 at 15% noise.
